t: 2813. Maximum Elegance of a K-Length Subsequence
o: Pick exactly k items maximizing (sum of profits) + (distinct categories)². Strategy: take the k most profitable items first (any optimal solution can be rearranged to include them — exchange argument), record which categories are duplicated, then iteratively replace the least-profitable duplicate with the best unused item of a brand-new category: each such swap changes elegance by (newProfit − dupProfit) + 2d + 1, which is positive whenever newProfit + 2d + 1 > dupProfit. Examples: [[3,2],[5,1],[10,1]], k=2 → 13+4=17; [[3,1],[3,1],[2,2],[5,3]], k=3 → 10+9=19.
k: An optimal answer exists containing the k highest-profit items; duplicates among them form a replacement pool.
Swapping a duplicate (profit q) for a new-category item (profit p) gains p − q + 2d + 1 — note the 2d+1 term can make even a lower-profit swap worthwhile.
Greedy: repeatedly perform the most beneficial swap until none improves the objective.

a.i: Sort by profit descending, take top k, track duplicated profits in a sorted list and the best remaining profit per unseen category. While a swap improves (p − q + 2d + 1 > 0), apply it and update the answer.
s: Sort descending by profit; take first k, collecting duplicates.
Map each category not yet covered to its best remaining profit; sort those descending.
While beneficial, swap smallest duplicate for next best new-category profit; track max elegance.
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting dominates; the greedy sweep is linear.
a.sp: O(n) for the duplicate list and per-category best map.

w: This is the standard interview solution. The subtle point interviewers probe: the swap condition must include the +2d+1 marginal square gain — dropping it fails cases like [[5,1],[5,1],[5,2]], k=2 (expected 14). Also note the answer is taken as a max over all prefixes of swaps, since the quadratic term isn't monotonic in profit trade-offs. Follow-up: maximize profit + c·distinct² for arbitrary c, or stream items online.
